summary: Describes how a certification authority in the RPKI does a planned change of its key pair, and what it means for relying parties that keep a local cache of the repository. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: Just as you change the locks on your house from time to time, a certificate authority swaps its key. This explains the steps so everyone else keeps trusting it.

questions: how to roll over an rpki key
how long is the rpki staging period
how does a ca roll over its key
what must relying parties do during key rollover
subtitle: How a certification authority in the RPKI swaps its key pair without breaking anyone who validates its objects.

tldr.problem: An RPKI certification authority needs to change its key pair from time to time, but relying parties that cache the repository must be able to validate every authentic object at all times, with no gap in which they reach wrong conclusions.
tldr.mechanism: The CA creates a NEW instance of itself with a new key pair, waits through a Staging Period of at least 24 hours so everyone can fetch the new certificate, then reissues all subordinate products under the new key and retires the old instance.
tldr.outcome: Rollover is invisible to subordinate CAs and keeps the pointers in certificates intact, at the cost of extra work for the CA and a requirement that relying parties re-synchronize at least every 24 hours.

today: RFC 6489 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 174), and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the published procedure for planned CA key rollover in the RPKI.

sections.title: Why a Conservative Rollover
sections.content:
RFC 6489 describes the algorithm a Certification Authority (CA) in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) uses to roll over its key pair. It builds on the RPKI architecture in RFC 6480 and assumes the reader knows the certificate profile in RFC 6487 and the repository structure in RFC 6481.

The procedure is called conservative because the CA's actions are not meant to disrupt relying parties (RPs), the systems that keep a local cache of the RPKI repository. With this procedure, RPs can validate all authentic objects in the RPKI at all times.

The focus is a planned rollover, not an emergency one caused by a suspected key compromise. The same procedure still applies in an emergency, except for the length of the Staging Period.
sections.eli5: Swapping a key has to be done carefully, so that everyone who checks the club's papers can keep checking them the whole time.

sections.title: One Key, One CA Instance
sections.content:
A CA instance is associated with a single key pair. Strictly speaking, a CA therefore never rolls its key. Instead it creates a "new" instance of itself with a new key pair and substitutes it into the RPKI hierarchy in place of the "old" one.

The two instances share one repository publication point, but each has its own CRL and its own manifest. The RFC names three states:

  • CURRENT: the active instance that accepts and processes certificate issuance and revocation requests.
  • NEW: the instance being created. It is not active and does not process requests. It SHOULD issue a CRL and an EE certificate for its manifest, so that it is a trivial, complete and consistent CA.
  • OLD: an instance being removed. It cannot process requests, but keeps issuing regularly scheduled CRLs and an EE certificate to update its manifest.
sections.eli5: The CA does not change its key. It builds a twin with a new key, and the twin slowly takes over the old one's job.

sections.title: The Six Rollover Steps
sections.content:
The CA MUST perform six steps in order, run through to completion, and unless stated otherwise each step SHOULD happen without intervening delay.

  1. Generate a new key pair for the NEW CA. It MUST differ from the CURRENT CA's pair.
  2. Send a certificate request to the issuer of the CURRENT CA certificate. It MUST include the same SIA extension as the CURRENT certificate. The resulting NEW CA certificate has a subject name chosen by the issuer, which MUST differ from the CURRENT subject name.
  3. After the NEW CA certificate is published, publish an initially empty CRL for the NEW CA, then a manifest listing only that CRL. The manifest is signed with a single-use EE certificate whose private key is destroyed afterwards.
  4. Enter the Staging Period. During it the NEW CA SHOULD reissue, but not publish, everything issued under the CURRENT CA.
  5. When the Staging Period ends, the NEW CA MUST publish the reissued products, replacing the corresponding ones. The NEW CA's manifest now lists them all. CURRENT becomes OLD, NEW becomes CURRENT, and the OLD CA issues a manifest listing only its own CRL.
  6. Request revocation of the OLD CA certificate. Once it is revoked, the OLD CA's CRL and manifest are removed from the repository and its private key is destroyed.

Step 5 is expected to be very brief, perhaps a few minutes, because the products were already reissued. It is still desirable that RPs see it as atomic.
sections.eli5: Make a new key, announce it, wait a day while quietly preparing everything, switch over in one quick move, then throw the old key away.

sections.title: The Staging Period and Relying Parties
sections.content:
The Staging Period gives all RPs time to download the NEW CA certificate before any certificates, CRLs or signed objects are published under it. Its length is the CA's decision, but it SHOULD be no less than 24 hours. Because it adds no burden for RPs, there is no recommended maximum. In an emergency rollover the CA decides whether 24 hours is appropriate or a shorter period is needed.

During this time the CURRENT CA SHOULD keep accepting certificate issuance requests and MUST keep accepting revocation requests. Anything issued by the CURRENT CA in the period MUST also be reissued under the NEW CA, and anything revoked MUST NOT be reissued.

The other half of the bargain is on the RP side: RPs that keep a local cache MUST synchronize with the distributed repository at regular intervals of no longer than 24 hours.
sections.eli5: The waiting day lets everyone pick up the new key. In return, everyone promises to check for news at least once a day.

sections.title: Reissuing Certificates and Signed Objects
sections.content:
The NEW CA MUST reissue every subordinate product. Except for manifests and CRLs, reissued products are published under the same repository object names, which overwrites the old ones. This keeps the AIA pointers of lower-tier products correct, so no subordinate CA has to do anything. CRLs and manifests are not reissued; they are generated per CA instance.

For CA certificates, all fields and extensions are copied from the old certificate. Only notBefore MAY be set to the current time and the serial number MAY change. Each certificate issued under a given CA instance MUST still have a unique serial number.

For RPKI signed objects (CMS signed-data objects as in RFC 6488), the EE certificate MUST be reissued under the NEW CA's key. The CA MAY copy it as for CA certificates and drop the new EE certificate into the CMS wrapper unchanged otherwise. Alternatively it MAY generate a new key pair for the EE certificate, in which case the content MUST be resigned, and the certificate MUST carry the new public key and a new notBefore. The presence or absence of the signing-time attributes MUST NOT affect validity.
sections.eli5: All the old papers are copied and restamped with the new key, using the same file names so nobody has to relabel their folders.

sections.title: How Often to Roll a Key
sections.content:
No key should be used forever: the longer it is in use, the more likely it has been compromised through carelessness, accident, espionage or cryptanalysis. Rolling too rarely is also risky, because the procedure may not be followed precisely, which raises the chance of operational failure.

Against that, rollover costs the CA and the population of RPs effort. When a CA rekeys it changes many signed objects, which affects every RP. A CA should therefore roll at regular intervals, frequent enough to limit compromise risk and keep its operators practiced, but with key lifetimes long enough that the load across the whole RPKI is not excessive.
sections.eli5: Locks should be changed now and then, but not so often that everybody is always busy fetching new keys.

viz.caption: CA INSTANCE ROLES DURING ROLLOVER (SIMPLIFIED FROM RFC 6489)
THE SIX STEPS IN ONE GLANCE

items.title: 1. New key pair
items.text: Must differ from the CURRENT pair.

items.title: 2. Certificate request
items.text: Same SIA extension; issuer picks a distinct subject name.

items.title: 3. Trivial NEW CA
items.text: Empty CRL and a manifest listing only that CRL.

items.title: 4. Staging Period
items.text: At least 24 hours; reissue but do not publish.

items.title: 5. Switch
items.text: Publish reissued products; CURRENT becomes OLD.

items.title: 6. Retire OLD
items.text: Revoke the OLD certificate and destroy its key.
